text:
The metropolis, known as Neo-Veridia, was not merely a city but a living, breathing organism of steel and silicon, constructed over the ruins of the Old World’s collapse. Its history is etched into the very foundations: a century ago, the Great Data Flood submerged the coastal plains, forcing humanity to build upward. The skyscrapers, piercing the perpetual smog layer, are remnants of the Corporate Ascendancy era, their glass facades now scarred by acid rain and patched with holographic advertisements that flicker in rhythmic, hypnotic patterns. The air itself tastes of ozone and recycled exhaust, thick with the humidity of a climate-controlled dome that traps the heat of millions of bodies and servers. Below, the streets are a labyrinth of neon-lit alleyways and elevated walkways, where the hum of hovercars creates a constant, low-frequency vibration that rattles the teeth of those who walk the pavement. The digital billboards, towering hundreds of feet high, do not just sell products; they monitor mood, adjusting their content to manipulate the collective psyche of the populace, ensuring compliance through a subtle, pervasive dopamine loop.

Amidst this high-tech, low-life chaos, a single, archaic object sits on a rusted desk in a cramped apartment: a candle. Its primary material is beeswax, harvested from the last remaining hives in the vertical farms of the upper tiers. Unlike the synthetic paraffin or chemical gels used for industrial lighting, this beeswax is golden, translucent, and carries the faint, sweet scent of honey and pollen—a sensory relic from a time before the sky was permanently choked by smog. The wax is poured into a simple, hand-blown glass holder, its surface imperfect and warm to the touch. When lit, the flame does not flicker with the erratic energy of electric arcs but burns with a steady, organic glow, casting long, dancing shadows against the walls. It is a symbol of resistance, a small, fragile defiance against the cold, unyielding light of the neon city, representing a connection to nature and history in a world that has forgotten both.
